summary: A note that users of UCSB's Remote Job Server could submit jobs that actually ran at UCLA-CCN's job service, without converting to the UCLA protocol. It lists the disadvantages, including extra control language, a UCSB batch account, and separate submit and retrieve steps. It builds on RFC 436 and 477.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC describes submitting jobs to UCLA-CCN through UCSB's Remote Job Service. UCSB handles input and output, while UCLA schedules and runs the jobs.

subtitle: How UCSB users could submit jobs to UCLA-CCN through UCSB's RJS.

tldr.problem: Users wanted to access UCLA-CCN's Remote Job Service through UCSB's Network Standard RJS without converting to UCLA's protocol.
tldr.mechanism: UCSB's service handles local reading, printing, and punching while UCLA handles job scheduling, resources, and execution.
tldr.outcome: The arrangement avoids an intermediate host file but has separate submission and retrieval phases and other listed limitations.

sections.title: Routing Jobs from UCSB to UCLA
sections.content:
RFC 490 describes access to UCLA-CCN's Remote Job Service through UCSB's Network Standard RJS. It says users can avoid converting to the UCLA protocol and avoid creating files on an intermediate host.

UCSB handles reading, printing, and punching; UCLA handles scheduling, resource allocation, and job execution.
sections.plainLanguage: UCSB's service connects its users to UCLA's job service. The work runs at UCLA, while UCSB handles the job input and output.

sections.title: Separate Submission and Retrieval
sections.content:
Users submit a job with the READ command and retrieve print or punch output with PRINT or PUNCH. Submission and retrieval are separate phases, and usually require two UCSB jobs for one UCLA job.

Commands are issued through local job control language, and their actions and messages are recorded in the RJS log included with the user's listing.
sections.plainLanguage: First the user sends the job with READ. Later, PRINT or PUNCH retrieves its output, so the two steps are usually separate.

sections.title: Limitations and Operating Conditions
sections.content:
The RFC lists several disadvantages: additional job-control statements are needed to route work, a UCSB batch account must be opened, and turnaround includes waits in UCSB batch queues. It also says the current implementation requires separate submission and retrieval.

The UCLA RJS terminal used for transfers should not be accessed online until transfers to or from UCSB are complete.
sections.plainLanguage: The service adds queue time and requires a UCSB batch account. Users must also keep the UCLA RJS terminal free while transfers are in progress.
